These pages walk through Philip Tagg's book *Everyday Tonality II: Towards a Tonal Theory of What Most People Hear* (2014) in plain words. Tagg's point: most of the music people hear every day (pop, rock, film, games, folk) does not follow the rules of classical harmony, and needs its own words. Page numbers point to the book. The summaries were drafted with AI help from the book's text; check a page before quoting it. New words: [glossary](tagg-glossary.qmd).

## Chapter 3: Heptatonic modes (pp. 85–149)

A mode is a short list of the notes a piece of music uses, put in order inside one octave. "Heptatonic" means seven notes. Tagg argues that the major scale (which he calls the **ionian** mode) is just one mode among many. School theory treats it as normal and calls everything else "modal". He thinks that is unfair.

He walks through the seven "church" modes: ionian, dorian, phrygian, lydian, mixolydian, aeolian and locrian. Each has its own pattern of whole-tone and semitone steps, which gives it its own flavour. He shows that a mode does not decide the mood by itself. Aeolian can be gloomy in Gloomy Sunday or cheerful in God Rest You Merry, Gentlemen. A poll of "saddest songs" found most were in major keys.

The second half looks at modes from the Arab world, Turkey, Greece, Spain and the Balkans. Many have a "flat two" or a big step of an augmented second. These are often used in film and metal to make something sound "foreign" or "dark". Tagg argues listeners should hear them as the home sound of those places, not just as exotic spice.


### Key ideas
- A mode is a tonal vocabulary reduced to one of each note in an octave. A real tune uses its notes in a particular way, not like a scale run (p. 86).
- Classical theory treats ionian as the norm, so "minor" notes need a flat sign. Tagg calls bending other modes toward ionian "ionianisation" (p. 90).
- "Tonal versus modal" makes no sense. All modes are tonal (p. 93).
- Each church mode has a unique scale-degree profile. For example, only the dorian has a flat third, a major sixth and a flat seventh together (p. 96).
- The same mode can feel sad or happy. Speed, rhythm, timbre and culture all matter (p. 111).
- An Arab maqam is a mode plus rules for how to move through it. Its octave is split into two four-note groups called tetrachords (jins) (p. 118).
- "Phrygian dominant" and "lydian dominant" are misleading names. Those modes have no dominant (p. 129).


### Example pieces
- God Save The Queen: used to show how a real tune becomes a mode (p. 87)
- Scarborough Fair (Simon & Garfunkel): dorian (p. 100)
- The Simpsons theme (Danny Elfman): lydian flavour (p. 102)
- Barber's Adagio for Strings: phrygian (p. 101)
- Nirvana's Smells Like Teen Spirit and Lithium: aeolian (p. 109)
- Lawrence of Arabia (Maurice Jarre): a Western idea of "Arab-sounding" (p. 120)
- Y Viva España (Sylvia Vrethammar): tourist "flamenco" that is really in A minor (p. 132)


### Try this
On white keys only, play a drone (hold or repeat the note) on D, and make up short melodies that end on D. That is dorian. Now do the same on A (aeolian) and on C (ionian). For each, write one word for how it feels. Then listen to a song in your list and ask: does that feeling match what the song says? Tagg shows it often doesn't.

## Chapter 4: Non-heptatonic modes (pp. 151–178)

Most music theory counts scales with seven notes (heptatonic). Tagg's point in this chapter is that scales with fewer or more notes are not "incomplete" or "cluttered". Five-note scales are pentatonic, six-note scales are hexatonic, and eight-note scales are octatonic. Three- and four-note tunes (tritonic and tetratonic) are also common. Words like "thirdless hexatonic" only describe a trait, not a fault (p. 151).

The pentatonic modes are the most widespread outside classical music. Tagg names them by the note they centre on: doh (the "major" pentatonic), la (the "minor" pentatonic) and ré (a mode with no third at all, so it is neither major nor minor). Blues and gospel singers bend and swap some of these notes, which gives the blues sound. Rock riffs lean on the minor pentatonic all the time.

Hexatonic tunes are everywhere in British, Irish and American folk music and in some pop hits, yet they have no standard names. Tagg gives them names. The whole-tone and octatonic scales sound "unrooted", so film and TV use them for dreams, magic and mystery. Tagg ends by warning that using a scale to signal a place or a mood ("Celtic", "Spanish") is often a stereotype, though it can still work on audiences (pp. 176–178).


### Key ideas
- Pentatonic, hexatonic and octatonic modes are complete in their own right; the seven-note count is only a convention (p. 151).
- Anhemitonic pentatonic modes have no semitones; they are the notes you could play on the black keys of a piano (p. 153).
- Doh-, la- and ré-pentatonic differ in where the "home" note sits; ré-pentatonic has no third at all, so students often wrongly hear it as dorian minor (p. 157).
- Blues pentatonic modes take the doh or la mode and bend or swap notes (blue notes); the doh version is more "gospel", the la version more guitar blues and rock (pp. 158–163).
- Hexatonic modes are named doh-, la- or ré-hexatonic by the notes they leave out (seventhless, sixthless, thirdless) (pp. 165–173).
- The whole-tone and octatonic scales are non-tonical (no clear home note) and signal mystery in film and jazz (pp. 173–175).

**Example pieces the chapter uses**
- Sweet Home Alabama (Lynyrd Skynyrd) and Da Doo Ron Ron (The Crystals): vocal lines of only three notes (p. 152).
- Amazing Grace and Skye Boat Song: doh-pentatonic (p. 155). Hurt (Johnny Cash): la-pentatonic (p. 156).
- Smoke On The Water (Deep Purple): blues la-pentatonic riff (p. 163). Jolene (Dolly Parton) and Bus Stop (Hollies): la-hexatonic (pp. 171–172).
- Debussy's Voiles: whole-tone scale (p. 174).


### Try this
Play only the black keys on a piano and make up a short tune; that is a doh- or la-pentatonic melody. Then try to pick out Skye Boat Song on those keys (Tagg says it is on the black keys, p. 155). Next, listen to Smoke On The Water and find which riff notes are not part of an ordinary pentatonic scale (the "blue" note).

## Words from these chapters

**Doh-pentatonic**: The five-note mode that centres on doh; it is the "major pentatonic" and is the only one of the five with a major third. Amazing Grace is an example. (Tagg p. 155, 177)

**Hexatonic**: A mode with six different notes per octave, such as the seventhless doh-hexatonic or the sixthless la-hexatonic. (Tagg p. 165–166)

**ionian**: Tagg's word for the major scale. He avoids calling it the default or "normal", because it is only one mode among many. (Tagg p. 90)

**ionianisation**: The classical habit of treating the ionian mode as the norm, and bending other modes (such as minor) to fit it, for example by raising the seventh note. (Tagg p. 90)

**La-pentatonic**: The five-note mode that centres on la; it is the "minor pentatonic" and is used all over rock music. The blues version adds a flat five. (Tagg p. 156, 161)

**maqam**: The Arab idea of a mode, with extra rules about which notes to stress and how a melody should move. The octave is thought of as two tetrachords. (Tagg p. 114)

**mode**: A tonal vocabulary reduced to one occurrence of each note, put in order inside one octave. The major scale is one mode (the ionian). (Tagg p. 86)

**Octatonic scale**: An eight-note scale of alternating whole tones and semitones; film uses it for mystery and jazz players call it the "diminished scale". (Tagg p. 175)

**Pentatonic**: A mode with five different notes per octave. Anhemitonic pentatonic modes have no semitones and can be played on the black keys of a piano. (Tagg p. 151, 153)

**Quartal**: Mode or chord without a third; a "quartal" mode such as ré-pentatonic is neither major nor minor. (Tagg p. 166, 178)

**Ré-pentatonic**: A five-note mode centring on ré that has neither a major nor a minor third, so it is often wrongly heard as dorian. (Tagg p. 156–157)

**Whole-tone scale**: A six-note scale made of whole tones only; it has no perfect fifth or fourth, so it sounds unrooted and is used for dream or mystery scenes. (Tagg p. 173–174)
